The Hings sold the Starlite on a Tuesday, and the paperwork says exactly what
it always says. $410,000 total for the building, the fixtures, the name, and
the recipe box. Escrow closed at 9:40 in the morning. By 11:00 the new owners'
sign crew had measured the front glass, and by 2:15 a man in a gray
quarter-zip was reading the pie case with a light meter. I had the
counter seat nearest the register, a $3.25 coffee, and no assignment beyond
watching.

The buyer is a hospitality group out of Scottsdale with a press release that
deserves a public reading. "An elevated comfort concept honoring the site's
legacy." Honoring. This is the language of the embalming table — the
wretched, rouged, formaldehyde grammar of men who buy a thing precisely
because it was alive and intend to charge admission to the corpse. The
release runs 340 words and the word "diner" appears once, in quotation marks,
like a slur they are bravely reclaiming. There is a rot that works in
daylight and files trademarks, and it smells like fresh paint.

Suppose they move fast. Suppose the crew arrives Thursday with the reclaimed
barnwood and the Edison bulbs, and the menu goes to card stock, and the $4.75
two-egg plate comes back from consulting at $16 as heritage hens on artisan
sourdough — and suddenly the regulars are an aesthetic, the counter is
seating architecture, the coffee has tasting notes, visions of a
ribbon-cutting with a mayor and a hashtag, faster than the
paint can dry, the room hurtling toward a rebrand nobody at this counter
voted on. It could happen by Labor Day, and there is no way to know which
Thursday the barnwood lands. Check the permits; I did.

Here is what the walk-through sheet actually recorded. A long, low,
formica-scarred counter, eleven stools, four booths patched with tape the
color of a Band-Aid. A Bunn machine from 1987 that has outlived three health
inspectors. Ang Hing worked the flattop; his wife Marisol ran the register
and the room. "Forty-one years," he told me, wiping the steel like it still
needed it. "Same spatula for the last nineteen. You don't change what the
eggs like."

The Starlite used to be full at 6:15 in the morning. The counter at that hour
held linemen and night nurses and two detectives who never said what they
were working. Ang fed them all. The linemen are long gone now — the depot
closed years ago — and the nurses park at the new garage across town. What
was left, at the end, was the coffee and the habit of the room. That is not
nothing. It was the last honest $3.25 in the county.

The light-meter man ordered nothing.
